item.title: Responsibilism and culture
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02616-z

Previous research has widely associated East Asian cultures with higher levels of collectivism, which is often measured through self-report scales that emphasize warmth and prosociality towards all people. Talhelm et al. developed a responsibilism scale that captures duties and responsibilities in close relationships.
item.dc:title: Responsibilism and culture
item.dc:creator: Adam B. Cohen
Amiryah N. Toves

item.title: Recognizing Indigenous peoples
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02619-w

Settler states increasingly offer Indigenous peoples symbolic recognition, such as land acknowledgements, instead of political power or resources, yet the effects of these gestures are untested. Peyton and McNamee’s experiments in the USA and Australia find that land acknowledgements raise awareness of Indigenous peoples but reduce interest in learning more.
item.dc:title: Recognizing Indigenous peoples
item.dc:creator: Raymond I. Orr

item.title: Both selfish and prosocial actors distort their impact on others, but selfish-serving spin seems to spread
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02584-4

From consumers buying fair-trade products to policy makers funding science, people often do not know exactly how their actions will affect others. We show that selfish and prosocial actors alike may distort their impact in self-serving ways, but selfish-serving distortions catch on more readily than prosocial-serving distortions and increase followers’ selfishness.
item.dc:title: Both selfish and prosocial actors distort their impact on others, but selfish-serving spin seems to spread

item.title: Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
item.content:encoded:
Nature Human Behaviour, Published online: 12 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02611-4

Simulating a global survey of economic preferences across 74 countries, this study shows that large language models reproduce some demographic patterns in human preferences but fail to capture cultural differences, especially in lower-income countries.
item.dc:title: Simulated responses from large language models are weak proxies for human economic preferences across 74 countries
